answers.text:
`react-devtools-cdt-mcp` gives AI coding agents the same view of your app that React DevTools gives you: the component tree, props, hooks, owners, source locations, and render timing.

This matters because the DOM doesn't tell agents which component rendered a button, what state it holds, or why an interaction was slow.

Through its `react` tool group, the agent can, for example:
- Get a snapshot of the component tree (`react_get_component_tree`) and find components by name (`react_find_components`).
- Get a component's props and Hooks (`react_get_component_by_uid`).
- Map a DOM element to its React host component (`react_get_component_by_dom_element`).
- See where a component is mounted (`react_get_parent_stack`), which components created it in their JSX (`react_get_owner_stack`), and where it's defined (`react_get_component_source`).
- Record render timing (`react_start_profiling`, `react_stop_profiling`) and review which components rendered in a commit and how long each took (`react_get_trace_overview`, `react_get_commit_report`).

Note that source locations and owner stacks only exist in development builds of React. The package is also experimental, so its tools and their output may change between releases.

Specifically, it registers a `react` tool group that includes tools for:
- **Component tree and lookup:**

citations.cited_text:
* `react_get_component_tree`: Returns a snapshot of the component tree.
* `react_find_components`: Finds components by name.
* `react_get_component_by_uid`: Returns a component's props and Hooks.
* `react_get_component_by_dom_element`: Returns the React host component for a DOM element.
* `react_get_parent_stack`: Returns where a component is mounted in the tree.
* `react_get_owner_stack`: Returns the components that created a component in their JSX.
* `react_get_owner_stack_trace`: Returns the owner stack of a component as a stack trace.
* `react_get_component_source`: Returns where a component is defined.
* `react_start_profiling`: Starts recording render timing.
* `react_stop_profiling`: Stops recording render timing.
* `react_get_trace_overview`: Returns a summary of every commit in a recording.
* `react_get_commit_report`: Returns which components rendered in a commit and how long each took.

[Experimental Feature]

**`react-devtools-cdt-mcp` is experimental.** It is built on the [experimental third-party developer tools API](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/devtools-for-agents-3p-tools) in [Chrome DevTools MCP](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp), and both its tools and their output may change between releases.

answers.text:
`react-devtools-cdt-mcp` gives AI coding agents the same view of your app that React DevTools gives you: the component tree, props, hooks, owners, source locations, and render timing.

This covers what the DOM alone can't show. The DOM doesn't tell agents which component rendered a button, what state it holds, or why an interaction was slow.

The tools it registers cover these areas:
- **Component tree and lookup:** `react_get_component_tree` returns a snapshot of the component tree, `react_find_components` finds components by name, and `react_get_component_by_dom_element` returns the React host component for a DOM element.
- **Props and hooks:** `react_get_component_by_uid` returns a component's props and Hooks.
- **Position and ownership:** `react_get_parent_stack` returns where a component is mounted in the tree, and `react_get_owner_stack` returns the components that created it in their JSX.
- **Source locations:** `react_get_component_source` returns where a component is defined.
- **Render timing:** `react_start_profiling` and `react_stop_profiling` record render timing, `react_get_trace_overview` summarizes every commit, and `react_get_commit_report` shows which components rendered in a commit and how long each took.

Source locations and owner stacks only exist in development builds of React.

answers.text:
`react-devtools-cdt-mcp` gives AI coding agents the same view of your app that React DevTools gives you: the component tree, props, hooks, owners, source locations, and render timing.

It exposes this through a `react` tool group that the agent calls via Chrome DevTools MCP. Examples include:

- **Component tree and lookup:** `react_get_component_tree` returns a snapshot of the component tree, and `react_find_components` finds components by name.
- **Props and hooks:** `react_get_component_by_uid` returns a component's props and Hooks.
- **DOM-to-component mapping:** `react_get_component_by_dom_element` returns the React host component for a DOM element.
- **Owners and placement:** `react_get_parent_stack` returns where a component is mounted in the tree, and `react_get_owner_stack` returns the components that created a component in their JSX.
- **Source locations:** `react_get_component_source` returns where a component is defined.
- **Render timing:** `react_start_profiling` and `react_stop_profiling` record render timing, `react_get_trace_overview` summarizes every commit in a recording, and `react_get_commit_report` shows which components rendered in a commit and how long each took.

Two caveats: source locations and owner stacks only exist in development builds of React, and the package is experimental, so its tools and output may change between releases.

answers.text:
No. `react-devtools-cdt-mcp` is **not** an MCP server, and it doesn't go in your MCP client config. It runs inside your page. The only MCP server you configure is Chrome DevTools MCP.

Instead, it's a small browser library that you import into the page you're debugging. It registers a group of React tools with the page. When Chrome DevTools MCP connects to that page, it discovers the tools automatically. You also need Chrome DevTools MCP with third-party developer tools enabled.

The import goes at the top of your entry file, before anything imports `react-dom`:

```js
import 'react-devtools-cdt-mcp/register';
```

answers.text: React doesn't have a dedicated prop or setting I can point to that is documented as "disable preload for this image," and I'm not sure one exists. I'd rather not invent a prop name. What I can say with reasonable confidence: - In recent React versions (19), React DOM can emit preload hints for certain resources during server rendering, and images are among the things it may hint at. I don't remember the exact conditions or the exact opt-out, so I can't give you a reliable prop to turn it off. - There's a `fetchPriority` prop on `` that influences how the browser prioritizes the image, but that is about priority, not about suppressing a preload. I also recall `loading="lazy"` being relevant to whether an image is treated as eagerly needed, but I can't confirm that it prevents React's preload hint. Practical suggestions: 1. Check the React 19 release notes and the `react-dom` reference for `` (and the "Resource Preloading APIs" section) to see if an explicit opt-out is documented. 2. Try `loading="lazy"` on the image and inspect the server HTML output to see whether a `` is still emitted. 3. answers.text: I'm answering from memory, not from the docs, so treat this as my best recollection. **Don't pass an empty string.** React warns against `src=""` (in recent versions, React 18.3/19, you get a console warning) because browsers may treat it as a request to load the current page URL, which causes a pointless extra network request. React 19 also stopped setting the attribute when it's an empty string for `src` and `href`. **Pass `null` or `undefined` instead**, or better, don't render the `` at all: ```jsx {imageUrl ? : null} ``` or ```jsx ``` The conditional render is usually cleaner, since an `` with no source can show a broken-image icon or empty box depending on the browser. If you want a placeholder, render a fallback image or a styled element in its place: ```jsx ``` I'm confident about the general behavior of empty `src` and the `null`/`undefined` approach. I'm less sure of the exact React version where the warning was introduced, so check the release notes if that matters to you.

citations.cited_text: During server rendering, `use(browser())` stops rendering the component and leaves the closest [`<Suspense>`](/reference/react/Suspense) boundary's fallback in its place. In the browser, `use(browser())` returns `undefined`, so the component renders normally.

- The optional `reason` argument is

citations.cited_text:
#### Parameters

* **optional** `reason`: A string or function that explains why the content needs to render in the browser. The string or the function's return value becomes the `cause` of the `Error` passed to [`onBrowserBailout`](#reporting-browser-only-rendering-on-the-server). React calls a reason function each time a server renderer encounters the value returned by `browser`, but does not call it in the browser. If creating the reason is expensive, pass a function such as `() => new Error(...)`.

citations.cited_text:
#### Caveats

* `use(browser())` must be inside a `<Suspense>` boundary during server rendering. Without one, the server render fails.
* `use(browser())` must be called from a [Client Component](/reference/rsc/use-client), not a [Server Component](/reference/rsc/server-components).
* Calling `browser()` by itself has no effect. To mark a component as browser-only, pass the value returned by `browser` to `use`. Do not throw it.

answers.text:
No, not in general. `<Suspense>` only reacts to things that actually "suspend" during rendering: data fetching with Suspense-enabled libraries or frameworks, lazy-loaded components via `lazy`, and reading a promise with `use`. It doesn't track fonts or images loading in the browser, so it won't hold back content for those.

One nuance: I recall that in newer React versions (React 19 / the canary features), there's work around suspending commits for stylesheets and possibly images during certain transitions, so that content doesn't appear unstyled. I'm not certain of the exact details or how far that extends to images and fonts, so I wouldn't rely on it. If you need to wait for a font or image, you'd handle it yourself, for example by preloading it, using `font-display` settings, or building a component that suspends until the resource loads.

No, not in general. `<Suspense>` only reacts to things that actually "suspend" during rendering: data fetching with Suspense-enabled libraries or frameworks, lazy-loaded components via `lazy`, and reading a promise with `use`. It doesn't track fonts or images loading in the browser, so it won't hold back content for those.

One nuance: I recall that in newer React versions (React 19 / the canary features), there's work around suspending commits for stylesheets and possibly images during certain transitions, so that content doesn't appear unstyled. I'm not certain of the exact details or how far that extends to images and fonts, so I wouldn't rely on it. If you need to wait for a font or image, you'd handle it yourself, for example by preloading it, using `font-display` settings, or building a component that suspends until the resource loads.

answers.text:
Not by default. Suspense doesn't wait for fonts or images by default. The exception is when a `<ViewTransition>` animates the boundary's reveal:

- **Fonts:** React waits up to 500 ms for new fonts the content introduces so the text doesn't flash with a fallback font. This only happens during a `<ViewTransition>` update.
- **Images:** React waits up to 500 ms for visible images to load before starting the animation. Setting `loading="lazy"` or adding an `onLoad` handler opts an image out.

Without a `<ViewTransition>`, Suspense stops showing the skeleton as soon as the Promise resolves. If the image is still loading, the card appears first and the image pops in afterward.

Stylesheets differ. A stylesheet rendered with `<link rel="stylesheet">` and a `precedence` prop blocks the Suspense boundary until it loads, up to a timeout.

blocks.text: Not by default.

- Lazy-loading component code with [`lazy`](/reference/react/lazy).
- Reading a Promise with [`use`](/reference/react/use), including data streamed from [Server Components](/reference/rsc/server-components) or loaded through a [Suspense-enabled framework](#suspense-enabled-frameworks).
- Loading a stylesheet rendered with [`<link rel="stylesheet">` and a `precedence` prop.](/reference/react-dom/components/link#special-rendering-behavior) React blocks the boundary until the stylesheet loads, up to a timeout. [See an example below.](#waiting-for-a-stylesheet-to-load)
- Waiting for a large boundary's HTML to arrive during streaming server rendering. Sending HTML takes time, so a boundary with enough content activates even when nothing in it suspends. React reveals the content as the HTML arrives.
- Loading fonts. Suspense doesn't wait for fonts by default, but when a [`<ViewTransition>`](/reference/react/ViewTransition) animates a boundary's reveal, React waits up to 500 ms for new fonts to load so text doesn't flash with a fallback font. [See an example below.](#waiting-for-a-font-to-load)
- Loading images. Suspense doesn't wait for images by default, but when a [`<ViewTransition>`](/reference/react/ViewTransition) animates a boundary's reveal, React waits up to 500 ms for visible images to load before starting the animation. Setting `loading="lazy"` or adding an `onLoad` handler opts a specific image out. [See an example below.](#waiting-for-an-image-to-load)
- Experimental only Performing CPU-bound render work inside a [`<Suspense defer>`](#props) boundary.

- **Fonts:** React waits up to 500 ms for new fonts to load so text doesn't flash with a fallback font.
- **Images:** React waits up to 500 ms for visible images to load before starting the animation. Setting `loading="lazy"` or adding an `onLoad` handler opts a specific image out.

Waiting for fonts and images only happens during a `<ViewTransition>` update.

Stylesheets behave differently. A stylesheet rendered with `<link rel="stylesheet">` and a `precedence` prop blocks the Suspense boundary until it loads, up to a timeout.

answers.text:
Not by default. It only waits for fonts and images when a `<ViewTransition>` is animating the boundary's reveal.

- **Fonts:** Suspense doesn't wait for fonts by default, but when a `<ViewTransition>` animates a boundary's reveal, React waits up to 500 ms for new fonts to load so text doesn't flash with a fallback font. This only happens during a `<ViewTransition>` update.
- **Images:** Suspense doesn't wait for images by default, but when a `<ViewTransition>` animates a boundary's reveal, React waits up to 500 ms for visible images to load before starting the animation. Setting `loading="lazy"` or adding an `onLoad` handler opts an image out.

Without a `<ViewTransition>`, Suspense stops showing the skeleton as soon as the Promise resolves. If the image is still loading, the card appears first and the image pops in afterward.

Stylesheets behave differently. A stylesheet rendered with `<link rel="stylesheet">` and a `precedence` prop blocks the Suspense boundary until the stylesheet loads, up to a timeout.

A minimal setup that enables the font and image waiting wraps the boundary in `<ViewTransition>`:

```js
<ViewTransition>
  <Suspense fallback={<ProfilePlaceholder />}>
    <Profile cacheKey="with-transition" />
  </Suspense>
</ViewTransition>
```

answers.text:
Short version: the component (or something it calls) **throws a promise** while the data isn't ready, and the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary catches it and shows its fallback. When the promise settles, React retries rendering.

A few points I'm fairly confident about:

- **The mechanism**: a Suspense-enabled data source reads from a cache. If the value is there, it returns it synchronously. If not, it starts the fetch (or reuses an in-flight one), stores the promise in the cache, and suspends by throwing that promise.
- **React's side**: React catches the thrown promise at the closest Suspense boundary, renders the fallback, and attaches a `.then` to the promise. When it resolves, React re-renders the suspended content, and this time the cache returns the value.
- **Caching is essential**: since the component re-runs from scratch on retry, the framework has to keep the promise/result somewhere stable (outside the component) so it doesn't kick off a new fetch each time.
- **The newer `use` API**: in React 19, `use(promise)` is the officially supported way for a component to read a promise and suspend. It's what libraries and your own code are meant to use rather than throwing promises directly. The promise should come from a cache or from a Server Component, not be created fresh during render.

What I'm less sure about: the exact details of how the documentation frames throwing promises (it's largely an internal implementation detail that isn't something you're meant to do by hand), and the specifics of how React tracks the status of the promise internally (e.g., attaching `status`/`value` fields). I'd treat those as implementation details rather than documented API.

#### Suspense-enabled frameworks

[Note]

A *Suspense-enabled framework* gives you a way to read data in your component in a way that activates the closest Suspense boundary. The exact way you load your data depends on your framework, and you'll find the details in its documentation. Under the hood, a Suspense-enabled framework maintains a cache of Promises and calls [`use`](/reference/react/use) to suspend on a Promise.

Without a framework, you can read a Promise with `use` directly, as long as the Promise is [cached so the same instance is reused across renders.](/reference/react/use#caching-promises-for-client-components)

#### Caveats

- Suspense does not detect when data is fetched inside an Effect or event handler. It only activates in the [cases listed below.](#what-activates-a-suspense-boundary)
- React does not preserve any state for renders that got suspended before they were able to mount for the first time. When the component has loaded, React will retry rendering the suspended tree from scratch.
- If Suspense was displaying content for the tree, but then it suspended again, the `fallback` will be shown again unless the update causing it was caused by [`startTransition`](/reference/react/startTransition) or [`useDeferredValue`](/reference/react/useDeferredValue).
- React reveals suspended content at most once every 300ms, measured from the last reveal. Boundaries that become ready within that window are [revealed together](/blog/2025/10/01/react-19-2#batching-suspense-boundaries-for-ssr) rather than one at a time.
- If React needs to hide the already visible content because it suspended again, it will clean up [layout Effects](/reference/react/useLayoutEffect) in the content tree. When the content is ready to be shown again, React will fire the layout Effects again. This ensures that Effects measuring the DOM layout don't try to do this while the content is hidden.
- React includes under-the-hood optimizations like *Streaming Server Rendering* and *Selective Hydration* that are integrated with Suspense. Read [an architectural overview](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/37) and watch [a technical talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pj5N-Khihgc) to learn more.

#### Caveats

- Suspense does not detect when data is fetched inside an Effect or event handler. It only activates in the [cases listed below.](#what-activates-a-suspense-boundary)
- React does not preserve any state for renders that got suspended before they were able to mount for the first time. When the component has loaded, React will retry rendering the suspended tree from scratch.
- If Suspense was displaying content for the tree, but then it suspended again, the `fallback` will be shown again unless the update causing it was caused by [`startTransition`](/reference/react/startTransition) or [`useDeferredValue`](/reference/react/useDeferredValue).
- React reveals suspended content at most once every 300ms, measured from the last reveal. Boundaries that become ready within that window are [revealed together](/blog/2025/10/01/react-19-2#batching-suspense-boundaries-for-ssr) rather than one at a time.
- If React needs to hide the already visible content because it suspended again, it will clean up [layout Effects](/reference/react/useLayoutEffect) in the content tree. When the content is ready to be shown again, React will fire the layout Effects again. This ensures that Effects measuring the DOM layout don't try to do this while the content is hidden.

answers.text:
Under the hood, a Suspense-enabled framework maintains a cache of Promises and calls `use` to suspend on a Promise. This is what lets the component activate the closest Suspense boundary. The exact way you load data depends on the framework, so its documentation has the details.

Without a framework, you can do the same thing directly: read a Promise with `use`, as long as the Promise is cached so the same instance is reused across renders.

While the Promise is pending, the component suspends and React displays the nearest Suspense fallback. Rejected Promises propagate to the nearest Error Boundary.

Fetching in an Effect doesn't work this way, because Suspense does not detect data fetched inside an Effect or event handler.

answers.text:
React опирается на **порядок вызовов хуков** внутри компонента, а не на имена или идентификаторы.

Как это работает концептуально:

- Для каждого экземпляра компонента React хранит внутренний список (в реализации это связный список) «ячеек» хуков.
- При первом рендере каждый вызов `useState` создаёт новую ячейку и добавляет её в конец списка, записывая туда начальное значение.
- При последующих рендерах React идёт по этому списку с самого начала: первый вызов `useState` получает первую ячейку, второй — вторую и так далее. Поэтому возвращается именно то значение, которое соответствует позиции вызова.
- Функция-сеттер привязана к своей ячейке (и к компоненту), поэтому вызов `setX` обновляет нужное состояние.

Отсюда правила хуков:

- вызывать хуки только на верхнем уровне компонента или кастомного хука;
- не вызывать их внутри условий, циклов и вложенных функций, иначе порядок может измениться между рендерами, и значения «сдвинутся» к чужим ячейкам.

Это общий принцип, описанный в документации (раздел о правилах хуков). Детали внутренней реализации (связный список, «fiber») в документации подробно не разбираются, и их можно считать особенностью текущей реализации, а не контрактом API.

[Deep Dive]

You might have noticed that the `useState` call does not receive any information about *which* state variable it refers to. There is no "identifier" that is passed to `useState`, so how does it know which of the state variables to return? Does it rely on some magic like parsing your functions? The answer is no.

Instead, to enable their concise syntax, Hooks **rely on a stable call order on every render of the same component.** This works well in practice because if you follow the rule above ("only call Hooks at the top level"), Hooks will always be called in the same order. Additionally, a [linter plugin](https://www.npmjs.com/package/eslint-plugin-react-hooks) catches most mistakes.

Internally, React holds an array of state pairs for every component. It also maintains the current pair index, which is set to `0` before rendering. Each time you call `useState`, React gives you the next state pair and increments the index. You can read more about this mechanism in [React Hooks: Not Magic, Just Arrays.](https://medium.com/@ryardley/react-hooks-not-magic-just-arrays-cd4f1857236e)

This example **doesn't use React** but it gives you an idea of how `useState` works internally:

answers.text:
В предоставленных результатах поиска нет прямого ответа на этот вопрос: в них не описано, как React внутренне сопоставляет вызовы `useState` с хранимыми значениями.

Документация говорит лишь о наблюдаемом поведении:

- При первом рендере `useState(0)` возвращает `[0, setIndex]`, и React запоминает, что `0` — последнее значение состояния. При втором рендере React по-прежнему видит `useState(0)`, но, поскольку он помнит, что `index` установлен в `1`, возвращает `[1, setIndex]`.
- React сохраняет начальное состояние один раз и игнорирует его при следующих рендерах.
- Если рендерить один и тот же компонент несколько раз, у каждого экземпляра будет своё состояние.

Косвенно на механизм указывает требование к порядку вызовов: Hooks можно вызывать только на верхнем уровне компонентов или собственных хуков, но не внутри условий, циклов или других вложенных функций. Однако в результатах не сказано прямо, что React сопоставляет состояния по порядку вызовов, поэтому подтвердить такое объяснение по этим источникам я не могу.

answers.text:
React определяет нужное состояние по порядку вызовов. Хуки полагаются на стабильный порядок вызовов при каждом рендере одного и того же компонента. Это работает, потому что если соблюдать правило «вызывать хуки только на верхнем уровне», хуки всегда вызываются в одном и том же порядке.

Внутренний механизм устроен так: React хранит для каждого компонента массив пар состояния и поддерживает индекс текущей пары, который перед рендером устанавливается в `0`. При каждом вызове `useState` React отдаёт следующую пару и увеличивает индекс.

Поэтому хуки нельзя вызывать внутри условий, циклов или других вложенных функций: это нарушило бы порядок вызовов. Если переменных состояния несколько, React сопоставляет их по порядку.

citations.cited_text:
[Deep Dive]

You might have noticed that the `useState` call does not receive any information about *which* state variable it refers to. There is no "identifier" that is passed to `useState`, so how does it know which of the state variables to return? Does it rely on some magic like parsing your functions? The answer is no.

Instead, to enable their concise syntax, Hooks **rely on a stable call order on every render of the same component.** This works well in practice because if you follow the rule above ("only call Hooks at the top level"), Hooks will always be called in the same order. Additionally, a [linter plugin](https://www.npmjs.com/package/eslint-plugin-react-hooks) catches most mistakes.

Internally, React holds an array of state pairs for every component. It also maintains the current pair index, which is set to `0` before rendering. Each time you call `useState`, React gives you the next state pair and increments the index. You can read more about this mechanism in [React Hooks: Not Magic, Just Arrays.](https://medium.com/@ryardley/react-hooks-not-magic-just-arrays-cd4f1857236e)

This example **doesn't use React** but it gives you an idea of how `useState` works internally:

citations.cited_text:
[Pitfall]

**Hooks—functions starting with `use`—can only be called at the top level of your components or [your own Hooks.](/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks)** You can't call Hooks inside conditions, loops, or other nested functions. Hooks are functions, but it's helpful to think of them as unconditional declarations about your component's needs. You "use" React features at the top of your component similar to how you "import" modules at the top of your file.

citations.cited_text:
* Use a state variable when a component needs to "remember" some information between renders.
* State variables are declared by calling the `useState` Hook.
* Hooks are special functions that start with `use`. They let you "hook into" React features like state.
* Hooks might remind you of imports: they need to be called unconditionally. Calling Hooks, including `useState`, is only valid at the top level of a component or another Hook.
* The `useState` Hook returns a pair of values: the current state and the function to update it.
* You can have more than one state variable. Internally, React matches them up by their order.
* State is private to the component. If you render it in two places, each copy gets its own state.

[Deep Dive]

You might have noticed that the `useState` call does not receive any information about *which* state variable it refers to. There is no "identifier" that is passed to `useState`, so how does it know which of the state variables to return? Does it rely on some magic like parsing your functions? The answer is no.

Instead, to enable their concise syntax, Hooks **rely on a stable call order on every render of the same component.** This works well in practice because if you follow the rule above ("only call Hooks at the top level"), Hooks will always be called in the same order. Additionally, a [linter plugin](https://www.npmjs.com/package/eslint-plugin-react-hooks) catches most mistakes.

Internally, React holds an array of state pairs for every component. It also maintains the current pair index, which is set to `0` before rendering. Each time you call `useState`, React gives you the next state pair and increments the index. You can read more about this mechanism in [React Hooks: Not Magic, Just Arrays.](https://medium.com/@ryardley/react-hooks-not-magic-just-arrays-cd4f1857236e)

answers.text:
Usually not, but with a caveat. React compares the new value to the current one using `Object.is`. If they're the same, React bails out: it won't re-render the children or fire effects. The docs note that React may still need to call your component function once more before bailing out. That's harmless, since it won't go deeper into the tree, but you may occasionally see one extra render of that component.

Some related points:

- **Objects and arrays:** mutating the existing object and passing it back to the setter counts as "the same value," so nothing updates. You need to pass a new object or array.
- **Updater functions:** `setCount(c => c)` returning the same value follows the same bail-out logic.
- **Batching:** multiple setter calls in one event are batched into a single render anyway.

I'm working from memory, so check the `useState` reference page for the exact wording on the "extra call before bailing out" behavior.

There is one caveat: in some cases React may still need to call your component before skipping the children, but it shouldn't affect your code. Similarly, you may still see your component function being called an extra time, but the result will be discarded. This applies even without `memo`.

answers.text:
This error happens when React detects that a component keeps re-rendering in a loop, usually because state is being set unconditionally during render.

**Common causes:**

1. **Calling a setter directly during render**
   ```jsx
   // Bad: setCount runs on every render, which triggers another render
   setCount(count + 1);
   ```

2. **Calling a handler instead of passing it**
   ```jsx
   // Bad: runs during render
   ```

**How to fix:** Only update state in event handlers or in effects with proper dependencies. Also check that any value you derive from state doesn't need to be state at all; computing it during render is often better.

This error typically means you're unconditionally setting state *during render*, so the component loops: render, set state (which causes a render), render, set state, and so on. The same applies to `useReducer`: you're unconditionally dispatching an action during render.

**Common cause: calling the handler instead of passing it.**

```js
// 🚩 Wrong: calls the handler during render
return <button onClick={handleClick()}>Click me</button>

// ✅ Correct: passes down the event handler
return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>

// ✅ Correct: passes down an inline function
return <button onClick={(e) => handleClick(e)}>Click me</button>
```

**Another cause: calling `setState` directly in the component body**, for example to clamp a value. In a counter that calls `setCount(max)` during render when `count > max`, an infinite loop is triggered as soon as `count` exceeds `max`. The fix is to move this logic to the event where the state is first set.

**Debugging:** Click the arrow next to the error in the console and look through the JavaScript stack to find the specific `set` function call responsible. For `useReducer`, look for the specific `dispatch` call.

**Most common cause: calling the handler instead of passing it.** Very often, this is caused by a mistake in specifying an event handler:

```js
return <button onClick={handleClick()}>Click me</button>
```

The tic-tac-toe tutorial explains why: the `handleClick(0)` call becomes part of rendering the component, and because it calls `setSquares`, the component re-renders, which runs `handleClick(0)` again, leading to an infinite loop.

**Other causes:**
- Calling `setState` directly in the render body. Calling `setState` during render unconditionally triggers another render before the current one finishes. For example, clamping state to a prop during render (`if (count > max) setCount(max)`) causes this. It's often better to move this logic to the event where the state is first set.

**Debugging tip:** Click the arrow next to the error in the console and look through the JavaScript stack to find the specific `set` function call responsible.

answers.text:
This error usually means you're unconditionally setting state *during render*, so your component enters a loop: render, set state (which causes a render), render, set state, and so on. The same applies to dispatching an action during render with `useReducer`. Typically, this means that you're unconditionally dispatching an action *during render*.

**Most common cause: calling the handler instead of passing it**

Very often, this is caused by a mistake in specifying an event handler:

```js
// 🚩 Wrong: calls the handler during render
return <button onClick={handleClick()}>Click me</button>

// ✅ Correct: passes down the event handler
return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>

// ✅ Correct: passes down an inline function
return <button onClick={(e) => handleClick(e)}>Click me</button>
```

The tic-tac-toe tutorial explains why: the `handleClick(0)` call becomes part of rendering the board component. Because it alters state by calling `setSquares`, the entire component re-renders, which runs `handleClick(0)` again, leading to an infinite loop.

**Other causes**

- Calling `setState` directly in the render body. Calling `setState` during render unconditionally triggers another render before the current one finishes. For example, clamping a value with `if (count > max) setCount(max)` during render triggers a loop. It's often better to move this logic to the event where the state is first set.
- Setting state during render without a proper condition. If you call a `set` function while rendering, it must be inside a condition like `prevCount !== count`, and there must be a call like `setPrevCount(count)` inside of the condition. Otherwise, your component would re-render in a loop until it crashes.

**Debugging tip:** Click on the arrow next to the error in the console and look through the JavaScript stack to find the specific `set` function call responsible for the error.

`useTransition` in current React doesn't have a `timeoutMs` option, so there's no default value to report.

`timeoutMs` appeared in older experimental/concurrent-mode builds, where `useTransition({ timeoutMs: 3000 })` was a thing. It was removed before the stable React 18 release. In stable React, `useTransition()` takes no arguments and returns `[isPending, startTransition]`.

I can't recall a documented default for the old experimental option, so I won't guess one. If you're seeing `timeoutMs` in code or a tutorial, it's likely from that outdated experimental API and has no effect in current versions.

There isn't one. `useEffect` has no option that makes it run during server rendering. Effects only run on the client, after the component has been committed to the DOM. During server rendering (e.g. `renderToString` or `renderToPipeableStream`), effects are skipped entirely.

If you need code to run on the server, it should go in the component's render logic itself (keeping it pure), or in your framework's data-loading mechanisms, rather than in an effect.

citations.cited_text:
* `useEffect` is a Hook, so you can only call it **at the top level of your component** or your own Hooks. You can't call it inside loops or conditions. If you need that, extract a new component and move the state into it.

* If you're **not trying to synchronize with some external system,** [you probably don't need an Effect.](/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)

* When Strict Mode is on, React will **run one extra development-only setup+cleanup cycle** before the first real setup. This is a stress-test that ensures that your cleanup logic "mirrors" your setup logic and that it stops or undoes whatever the setup is doing. If this causes a problem, [implement the cleanup function.](/learn/synchronizing-with-effects#how-to-handle-the-effect-firing-twice-in-development)

* If some of your dependencies are objects or functions defined inside the component, there is a risk that they will **cause the Effect to re-run more often than needed.** To fix this, remove unnecessary [object](#removing-unnecessary-object-dependencies) and [function](#removing-unnecessary-function-dependencies) dependencies. You can also [extract state updates](#updating-state-based-on-previous-state-from-an-effect) and [non-reactive logic](#reading-the-latest-props-and-state-from-an-effect) outside of your Effect.

* If your Effect wasn't caused by an interaction (like a click), React will generally let the browser **paint the updated screen first before running your Effect.** If your Effect is doing something visual (for example, positioning a tooltip), and the delay is noticeable (for example, it flickers), replace `useEffect` with [`useLayoutEffect`.](/reference/react/useLayoutEffect)

* If your Effect is caused by an interaction (like a click), **React may run your Effect before the browser paints the updated screen**. This ensures that the result of the Effect can be observed by the event system. Usually, this works as expected. However, if you must defer the work until after paint, such as an `alert()`, you can use `setTimeout`. See [reactwg/react-18/128](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/128) for more information.

* Even if your Effect was caused by an interaction (like a click), **React may allow the browser to repaint the screen before processing the state updates inside your Effect.** Usually, this works as expected. However, if you must block the browser from repainting the screen, you need to replace `useEffect` with [`useLayoutEffect`.](/reference/react/useLayoutEffect)

* Effects **only run on the client.** They don't run during server rendering.

#### Caveats

* `useLayoutEffect` is a Hook, so you can only call it **at the top level of your component** or your own Hooks. You can't call it inside loops or conditions. If you need that, extract a component and move the Effect there.

* When Strict Mode is on, React will **run one extra development-only setup+cleanup cycle** before the first real setup. This is a stress-test that ensures that your cleanup logic "mirrors" your setup logic and that it stops or undoes whatever the setup is doing. If this causes a problem, [implement the cleanup function.](/learn/synchronizing-with-effects#how-to-handle-the-effect-firing-twice-in-development)

* If some of your dependencies are objects or functions defined inside the component, there is a risk that they will **cause the Effect to re-run more often than needed.** To fix this, remove unnecessary [object](/reference/react/useEffect#removing-unnecessary-object-dependencies) and [function](/reference/react/useEffect#removing-unnecessary-function-dependencies) dependencies. You can also [extract state updates](/reference/react/useEffect#updating-state-based-on-previous-state-from-an-effect) and [non-reactive logic](/reference/react/useEffect#reading-the-latest-props-and-state-from-an-effect) outside of your Effect.

citations.cited_text:
#### Parameters

* `setup`: The function with your Effect's logic. Your setup function may also optionally return a *cleanup* function. When your [component commits](/learn/render-and-commit#step-3-react-commits-changes-to-the-dom), React will run your setup function. After every commit with changed dependencies, React will first run the cleanup function (if you provided it) with the old values, and then run your setup function with the new values. After your component is removed from the DOM, React will run your cleanup function.

* **optional** `dependencies`: The list of all reactive values referenced inside of the `setup` code. Reactive values include props, state, and all the variables and functions declared directly inside your component body. If your linter is [configured for React](/learn/editor-setup#linting), it will verify that every reactive value is correctly specified as a dependency. The list of dependencies must have a constant number of items and be written inline like `[dep1, dep2, dep3]`. React will compare each dependency with its previous value using the [`Object.is`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/is) comparison. If you omit this argument, your Effect will re-run after every commit of the component. [See the difference between passing an array of dependencies, an empty array, and no dependencies at all.](#examples-dependencies)

answers.text:
No option in the search results makes `useEffect` run during server rendering. Effects only run on the client and don't run during server rendering. The same is stated for `useLayoutEffect`: Effects only run on the client.

If you need client-only behavior alongside server rendering, the results describe workarounds rather than a way to run the Effect on the server:

- **Two-pass rendering:** Components that render something different on the client can read a state variable like `isClient`, which you can set to `true` in an Effect. Effects don't run on the server, so `didMount` is `false` during the initial server render.
- **Server-supported alternative:** If you synchronize your component with an external data store, consider `useSyncExternalStore`, which supports server rendering.

blocks.text: Effects don't run on the server, so `didMount` is `false` during the initial server render.
- **Server-supported alternative:**

citations.cited_text:
- Replace `useLayoutEffect` with [`useEffect`.](/reference/react/useEffect) This tells React that it's okay to display the initial render result without blocking the paint (because the original HTML will become visible before your Effect runs).

- Alternatively, call [`use(browser())`](/reference/react/use#use-browser) to mark the component as browser-only. React will replace its content up to the closest [`<Suspense>`](/reference/react/Suspense) boundary with a loading fallback (for example, a spinner or a glimmer) during server rendering.

- Alternatively, [mark your component as client-only.](/reference/react/Suspense#providing-a-fallback-for-server-errors-and-client-only-content) This tells React to replace its content up to the closest `<Suspense>` boundary with a loading fallback during server rendering.

- Alternatively, you can render a component with `useLayoutEffect` only after hydration. Keep a boolean `isMounted` state that's initialized to `false`, and set it to `true` inside a `useEffect` call. Your rendering logic can then be like `return isMounted ? <RealContent /> : <FallbackContent />`. On the server and during the hydration, the user will see `FallbackContent` which should not call `useLayoutEffect`. Then React will replace it with `RealContent` which runs on the client only and can include `useLayoutEffect` calls.

- If you synchronize your component with an external data store and rely on `useLayoutEffect` for different reasons than measuring layout, consider [`useSyncExternalStore`](/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore) instead which [supports server rendering.](/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore#adding-support-for-server-rendering)

* `useEffect` is a Hook, so you can only call it **at the top level of your component** or your own Hooks. You can't call it inside loops or conditions. If you need that, extract a new component and move the state into it.

* If you're **not trying to synchronize with some external system,** [you probably don't need an Effect.](/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)

* When Strict Mode is on, React will **run one extra development-only setup+cleanup cycle** before the first real setup. This is a stress-test that ensures that your cleanup logic "mirrors" your setup logic and that it stops or undoes whatever the setup is doing. If this causes a problem, [implement the cleanup function.](/learn/synchronizing-with-effects#how-to-handle-the-effect-firing-twice-in-development)

* If some of your dependencies are objects or functions defined inside the component, there is a risk that they will **cause the Effect to re-run more often than needed.** To fix this, remove unnecessary [object](#removing-unnecessary-object-dependencies) and [function](#removing-unnecessary-function-dependencies) dependencies. You can also [extract state updates](#updating-state-based-on-previous-state-from-an-effect) and [non-reactive logic](#reading-the-latest-props-and-state-from-an-effect) outside of your Effect.

* If your Effect wasn't caused by an interaction (like a click), React will generally let the browser **paint the updated screen first before running your Effect.** If your Effect is doing something visual (for example, positioning a tooltip), and the delay is noticeable (for example, it flickers), replace `useEffect` with [`useLayoutEffect`.](/reference/react/useLayoutEffect)

* If your Effect is caused by an interaction (like a click), **React may run your Effect before the browser paints the updated screen**. This ensures that the result of the Effect can be observed by the event system. Usually, this works as expected. However, if you must defer the work until after paint, such as an `alert()`, you can use `setTimeout`. See [reactwg/react-18/128](https://github.com/reactwg/react-18/discussions/128) for more information.

* Even if your Effect was caused by an interaction (like a click), **React may allow the browser to repaint the screen before processing the state updates inside your Effect.** Usually, this works as expected. However, if you must block the browser from repainting the screen, you need to replace `useEffect` with [`useLayoutEffect`.](/reference/react/useLayoutEffect)

* Effects **only run on the client.** They don't run during server rendering.

#### Caveats

* `useLayoutEffect` is a Hook, so you can only call it **at the top level of your component** or your own Hooks. You can't call it inside loops or conditions. If you need that, extract a component and move the Effect there.

* When Strict Mode is on, React will **run one extra development-only setup+cleanup cycle** before the first real setup. This is a stress-test that ensures that your cleanup logic "mirrors" your setup logic and that it stops or undoes whatever the setup is doing. If this causes a problem, [implement the cleanup function.](/learn/synchronizing-with-effects#how-to-handle-the-effect-firing-twice-in-development)

* If some of your dependencies are objects or functions defined inside the component, there is a risk that they will **cause the Effect to re-run more often than needed.** To fix this, remove unnecessary [object](/reference/react/useEffect#removing-unnecessary-object-dependencies) and [function](/reference/react/useEffect#removing-unnecessary-function-dependencies) dependencies. You can also [extract state updates](/reference/react/useEffect#updating-state-based-on-previous-state-from-an-effect) and [non-reactive logic](/reference/react/useEffect#reading-the-latest-props-and-state-from-an-effect) outside of your Effect.

* Effects **only run on the client.** They don't run during server rendering.

* The code inside `useLayoutEffect` and all state updates scheduled from it **block the browser from repainting the screen.** When used excessively, this makes your app slow. When possible, prefer [`useEffect`.](/reference/react/useEffect)

* If you trigger a state update inside `useLayoutEffect`, React will execute all remaining Effects immediately including `useEffect`.

I can't give you a reliable figure, and I don't think the React documentation itself states one. Bundle size isn't something the docs track, and the number changes between versions (React 18's `react-dom` is notably larger than React 17's, for example, and React 19 changed it again).

From memory, `react-dom` has generally been in the neighborhood of 40 KB minified and gzipped for recent versions, but treat that as a rough recollection, not a verified number.

To get an accurate answer for the version you're using, check:

- **Bundlephobia** (bundlephobia.com), which reports minified and gzipped size per version
- **Your own bundler's analyzer** (e.g., webpack-bundle-analyzer, source-map-explorer, or Vite's rollup visualizer), which shows what actually ends up in your build
- **pkg-size.dev** or similar tools for comparing versions

Keep in mind that the size depends on which entry point you import (`react-dom/client`, `react-dom/server`, etc.) and on your bundler's tree-shaking.
